sections.title: The Problem
points: Video processing, crawling, report generation, and large fanout can exceed request deadlines. Execution times can also vary widely.
Synchronous execution keeps the client connection open. Slow tasks consume API capacity while the client waits.

sections.title: The Solution
points: Save a job record. Put its reference in a queue. Return the job ID without waiting for execution.
Separate workers execute the job. They save its status and results.
Clients poll for status or receive a completion event. Accepting a job does not mean that the job has completed.

sections.title: Trade-offs
points: A queue holds incoming work during traffic peaks. Workers can scale separately from API servers.
Retries allow recovery from failures. They also require progress tracking, duplicate handling, and monitoring.
Queue capacity is finite. Limit incoming work and the number of waiting jobs.

sections.title: 1) Message queue
points: Choose a queue with suitable durability, ordering, and delivery behavior. Define visibility timeouts and handling for repeated failures.
Put job IDs and storage references in messages. Keep large media files in object storage.
A saved job must eventually reach the queue. An outbox or a recovery scan can close a failed publication gap.

sections.title: 2) Workers
points: A worker claims a job and records the attempt. It executes within resource and time limits, then saves the result.
Acknowledge delivery only after the required output is safely stored.
Renew ownership while a long task runs. Conditional updates must prevent an old worker from replacing a newer result.
Use separate worker pools when tasks need different hardware. GPU tasks and lightweight tasks should not require identical capacity.

sections.title: 3) End-to-end flow
points: The API validates the request and saves a pending job. It then ensures that the queue receives the job reference.
Workers change job status from pending to running, then to completed or failed. Conditional updates protect these transitions.
Completion notifications can fail or repeat. The status API returns the stored result when a client reconnects.
Save progress at useful checkpoints. Avoid a database write for every small operation.

diagrams.caption: Async Worker Pool Putting It Together

flows.title: Submit and execute a background job
steps: The server validates the client's request. It creates a pending job record in the database.
The server publishes the job ID to the Job Queue. The message can reference data stored elsewhere.
The server returns the job ID to the client without waiting for the task to finish.
A worker pulls the message from the queue. It fetches the job details from the database.
The worker sets the status to processing.
The worker stores the result in the database or object storage, as required.
The worker records completed or failed status. The client can retrieve this state with the job ID.

sections.title: 1) Failure and repeated failure
points: Retry temporary failures with exponential backoff and jitter.
Limit attempts. Move persistent failures to a dead-letter queue or inspection state. Keep their error details.
A worker crash causes ownership to expire or the queue to deliver the job again. Resume from saved checkpoints where possible.

diagrams.caption: Async Worker Pool Dead Letter Queue

flows.title: Retry failures and isolate repeatedly failing jobs
steps: The queue makes failed or abandoned work available for another attempt under its delivery policy.
A worker checks the job's saved state before it retries. It avoids repeating completed effects where possible.
A temporary failure schedules another attempt after the configured delay.
After the retry limit, the system moves the job to the dead-letter queue. Other workers continue processing healthy jobs.
An operator investigates the error before returning a corrected job to the main queue.

sections.title: 2) Duplicate work
points: A queue can deliver a task again after its side effect succeeds. At-least-once delivery does not prevent duplicate execution.
Give each logical job a stable ID. Use idempotent output locations and the same idempotency key for repeated downstream requests.
A started record does not prove that work completed. The first worker could have crashed before it produced a result.

flows.title: Reuse the existing job for a repeated request
steps: The producer receives a request with an idempotency key for the logical operation.
It checks the database or cache for an existing job with that key.
If the job exists, it returns the existing job ID. It does not create another logical job.
Otherwise, it records the job and key, then publishes the job to the queue. The key reservation must prevent concurrent duplicates.
A worker executes the job with side effects that tolerate retries. Request deduplication alone does not prevent repeated execution.

sections.title: 3) Backpressure and mixed workloads
points: Scale workers using queue depth, waiting time, and resource use. Limit new jobs when the system cannot meet completion targets.
Use separate queues or reserved capacity for urgent and bulk work. Long tasks must not block all short tasks.
Limit requests to external services separately from worker count. More workers must not exceed a dependency's rate limit.

sections.title: 4) Dependencies
points: Use a durable workflow or dependency graph for related jobs. Avoid workers that wait indefinitely for other workers.
Start a stage only after its required predecessors complete. Repeated completion events must not start duplicate stages.
Define cancellation, compensation, and failure handling for workflows that complete only some stages.

sections.title: Conclusion
points: Keep durable job state and reliable queue publication. Use recoverable worker ownership and side effects that tolerate retries.
Limit the backlog and report progress. These controls keep asynchronous work usable during overload or partial failure.
